facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: O Mother of the universe! If it be that Thou art not willing at all to grant me immortality, then grant me this boon that my death may not occur from any other than from one who is horse-faced.
facts.text: The Devi Bhagavata Purana states that an asura named Hayagriva acquired a boon of invulnerability from Mahamaya ensuring he could be killed only by another entity bearing a horse's head.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: In fact, Bhagavan had unintentionally laughed once in Lakshmi Devi's presence. Devi thought that Bhagavan was laughing at her and insulting her.
facts.text: According to the Devi Bhagavata Purana, Vishnu's decapitation was preordained by a curse from Goddess Lakshmi, who mistakenly believed Vishnu was laughing at her appearance when he smiled without speaking.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: So let Visvakarmâ take a horse's head and fix it on the headless body of Visnu. Then Bhagavân Hayagrîva will slay the vicious wicked Asura, for the good of the Devas.
facts.text: In the Devi Bhagavata Purana, the celestial architect Vishvakarma is instructed to sever the head of a horse and affix it to Vishnu's headless torso, creating Lord Hayagriva to defeat the horse-headed demon.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The earliest sculptural representation of Hayagrīva is found from a small architectural fragment belonging to 3rd century CE., now preserved at Bharat Kala Bhavan, Varanasi.
facts.text: A red sandstone architectural fragment dating to the 4th century CE preserved at Bharat Kala Bhavan in Varanasi represents one of the earliest known archaeological depictions of Hayagriva Vishnu in Indian sculpture.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: In the three cardinal niches of the ambulatory pathway wall are incarnations of Vishnu - Varaha in the south, Narasimha in the west, and Hayagriva in the North.
facts.text: At the 10th-century Lakshmana Temple in Khajuraho, dated to 954 CE and maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India, an image of Hayagriva is carved into the northern cardinal niche of the sanctum wall.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Standing on an isolated hill, popularly known as Manikut Parvat, this temple was rebuilt in CE 1583 by Koch king Raghudeva (CE 1581- 1603), over the foundation of the ancient temple ruins of 10th- 11th century CE.
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India, Guwahati Circle
facts.text: The Archaeological Survey of India protects the Hayagriva Madhava Temple in Hajo, Assam, which was rebuilt in 1583 CE by Koch king Raghudeva Narayan upon the 10th- to 11th-century stone basement of an earlier shrine.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The fourth head may be replaced by a horse (Hayagriva, another avatar of Vishnu) or a Chakrapurusha (the personified Sudarshana Chakra – the discus weapon of Vishnu).
facts.source_name: Archaeological Survey of India / National Museum
facts.text: Sculptural specimens of Vaikuntha Chaturmurti dating from the Gupta period onwards feature four heads of Vishnu, with the fourth cardinal or dorsal head rendered as a horse representing Hayagriva.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Vedanta Desika worshipped Hayagriva on the small hillock named Oushadagiri and composed the Hayagriva Stotram.
facts.text: Tradition at Thiruvendipuram near Cuddalore holds that the 13th-century polymath Swami Vedanta Desika received a divine vision of Hayagriva atop the Oushadagiri hillock and composed the devotional hymn Hayagriva Stotram there.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: The presiding deity of the mutt is Lakshmi Hayagriva, the horse-headed avatar of Vishnu associated with learning and wisdom.
facts.text: Institutional tradition of the Parakala Mutt in Mysuru holds that its central sacred idol of Lakshmi Hayagriva has been continually passed down through its lineage of pontiffs since the 14th century CE.
